title: Python Context Managers: The with Statement Handbook
summary: A complete study-notes guide to Python's context manager protocol — from the with statement and __enter__/__exit__ internals to contextlib decorators, suppress, ExitStack, and async with. Covers mechanics, real patterns, trade-offs, and the mistakes that silently leak resources.

chapters.title: Why Context Managers Exist
points: Problem: resources (files, locks, sockets, DB connections) must be released even when code raises — forgetting release leaks handles
Naive `f = open('x'); f.read(); f.close()` skips close() if read() raises
try/finally is the correct manual fix: `f = open('x')` then `try: ... finally: f.close()` — verbose and repeated at every call site
Context manager = reusable try/finally packaged behind one keyword
`with open('x') as f:` guarantees close on normal exit, exception, `return`, `break`, and `continue`
RAII comparison: C++ destructors run at scope exit; Python has no deterministic scope destruction for locals, so `with` fills the gap
CPython refcounting often closes files early by accident — that is an implementation detail, not a guarantee; PyPy/Jython do not do it. Never rely on it
ResourceWarning: unclosed file <_io.TextIOWrapper ...> is the interpreter telling you a `with` was missing
Context managers manage more than resources: they manage *state pairs* — set/restore, enter/leave, begin/commit
PEP 343 introduced `with` in Python 2.5 (via `from __future__ import with_statement`), standard from 2.6

chapters.title: The with Statement: Syntax and Semantics
points: Grammar: `with EXPR as VAR:` — EXPR evaluates to a context manager, VAR binds the *return value of __enter__*, not EXPR
`as VAR` is optional: `with lock:` is valid when __enter__ returns nothing useful
Multiple managers on one line: `with open('a') as a, open('b') as b:` — entered left-to-right, exited right-to-left
Nested `with` blocks are exactly equivalent to the comma form; the comma form does not lose exception safety if the second open() fails — the first is still closed
Parenthesized multi-line form (Python 3.10+, formally): `with (open('a') as a, open('b') as b):` — allows trailing commas and clean wrapping
VAR is a normal assignment target: tuple unpacking works — `with mgr() as (x, y):`
VAR survives the block — it is not scoped to the `with`; after `with open(p) as f:` the name `f` still exists but the file is closed
`with` is a statement, not an expression — cannot be used inline in a comprehension or lambda
Return inside `with` still runs __exit__ before the function actually returns
Common misread: `with a, b:` evaluates `b` only after `a.__enter__()` succeeds

chapters.title: The Protocol: __enter__ and __exit__
points: A context manager is any object defining `__enter__(self)` and `__exit__(self, exc_type, exc_value, traceback)`
Both are looked up on the *type*, not the instance — assigning `obj.__enter__ = f` does not work (implicit special-method lookup)
__enter__ return value is what `as` binds; returning `self` is the most common choice
__exit__ receives `(None, None, None)` on clean exit, or the live exception triple on error
__exit__ returning a truthy value **suppresses** the exception; returning None/False lets it propagate
Accidental suppression bug: `return True` at the end of __exit__ swallows every error — return nothing instead
Minimal example: class Timer with `__enter__` recording `time.perf_counter()` and `__exit__` printing elapsed
typing: `contextlib.AbstractContextManager` is the ABC; it supplies a default `__enter__` returning self and requires __exit__
`__exit__` runs even for `GeneratorExit`, `KeyboardInterrupt`, and `SystemExit` (all BaseException) — cleanup code must be fast and non-throwing
Raising a *new* exception inside __exit__ replaces the original, which becomes `__context__` in the chained traceback
Type hint shape: `def __exit__(self, exc_type: type[BaseException] | None, exc: BaseException | None, tb: TracebackType | None) -> bool | None:`

chapters.title: Desugaring: What with Compiles To
points: `with EXPR as VAR: BODY` is roughly: `mgr = EXPR; exit = type(mgr).__exit__; value = type(mgr).__enter__(mgr)`
Then `try: VAR = value; BODY except: if not exit(mgr, *sys.exc_info()): raise` / `else: exit(mgr, None, None, None)`
Key detail: `__exit__` is fetched *before* `__enter__` runs — a manager missing __exit__ fails before any setup happens
If `__enter__` raises, `__exit__` is NEVER called — setup must be all-or-nothing inside __enter__
Bytecode: `BEFORE_WITH` (3.11+) pushes the exit callable and the enter result; `WITH_EXCEPT_START` invokes __exit__ on the error path
Older bytecode names: `SETUP_WITH` / `WITH_CLEANUP_START` / `WITH_CLEANUP_FINISH` (≤3.10) — same semantics
Inspect it yourself: `import dis; dis.dis(compile('with a as b: pass', '<s>', 'exec'))`
The manager object is kept alive on the stack for the whole block, so it cannot be garbage collected mid-body
The `as` binding happens *inside* the try, so a failing unpack still triggers __exit__
Because it desugars to try/finally, `with` costs roughly one extra attribute lookup + two calls — negligible vs I/O, measurable in tight loops

chapters.title: Writing Class-Based Context Managers
points: Pattern: `__init__` stores config, `__enter__` acquires and returns the resource, `__exit__` releases it
Do work in __enter__ not __init__ so the object is reusable across multiple `with` blocks
Example — temporary directory chdir: save `os.getcwd()` in __enter__, `os.chdir(old)` in __exit__
Example — DB transaction: __enter__ opens transaction; __exit__ commits when exc_type is None, else rolls back and returns None to re-raise
Reentrancy: most managers are NOT reentrant; entering the same instance twice corrupts saved state (store state on a stack if you need it)
Reusable vs one-shot: `threading.Lock` is reusable; a generator-based manager is single-use
Add `__enter__`/`__exit__` to an existing class to make it `with`-able without changing its API
Subclass `contextlib.ContextDecorator` to let one manager also work as `@mgr` on a function
`contextlib.closing(obj)` wraps any object with a `.close()` — `with closing(urlopen(url)) as page:`
Idempotent release: guard __exit__ so a double-close does not raise
Store the exception in __exit__ for logging, but re-raise by returning None — never silently drop it

chapters.title: contextlib.contextmanager: The Generator Shortcut
points: `@contextmanager` turns a single-yield generator into a context manager — no class needed
Shape: setup code, `yield value`, teardown code; the yielded value is bound by `as`
The generator must yield **exactly once** — zero yields raises `RuntimeError: generator didn't yield`, two raise `generator didn't stop`
Exceptions in the body are thrown *into* the generator at the yield point via `gen.throw()`
Therefore teardown after a bare `yield` is SKIPPED on exception — wrap in try/finally: `try: yield x finally: cleanup()`
To suppress an exception with @contextmanager, catch it around the yield and `return` (do not re-raise) — returning True does nothing here
Example: `@contextmanager def timed(label): t=perf_counter(); try: yield finally: print(label, perf_counter()-t)`
Objects from @contextmanager are single-use — reusing one raises `RuntimeError: generator didn't yield` on second entry
`@contextmanager` results are also decorators (they inherit ContextDecorator): `@timed('run')` on a function works, and each call makes a fresh generator
Trade-off: generator form is shorter and reads top-to-bottom; class form is reusable, reentrant, introspectable, and easier to subclass
`contextlib.nullcontext(x)` is the do-nothing manager for optional resources: `cm = open(p) if p else nullcontext(sys.stdout)`

chapters.title: Suppressing Exceptions Deliberately
points: `contextlib.suppress(FileNotFoundError)` replaces the `try/except X: pass` boilerplate
`with suppress(FileNotFoundError): os.remove(path)` — clearer intent than a bare except
Accepts multiple types: `suppress(KeyError, IndexError)`
Suppression aborts the rest of the block — statements after the raising line do not run; it is not `continue`
Never use `suppress(Exception)` as a catch-all; it hides bugs and makes debugging opaque
suppress catches subclasses too — `suppress(OSError)` also swallows FileNotFoundError and PermissionError
It cannot suppress exceptions raised outside its block, and it does not retry
Under the hood it is a class whose __exit__ returns `exc_type is not None and issubclass(exc_type, self._exceptions)`
`suppress` is reentrant and reusable — safe to make one instance a module constant
Comparison row: try/except lets you log or recover; suppress only discards — choose suppress when there is genuinely nothing to do
Python 3.12+: suppress also handles matching exceptions inside an `ExceptionGroup`, re-raising the unmatched remainder

chapters.title: ExitStack: Dynamic and Variable-Count Cleanup
points: Problem ExitStack solves: number of managers is unknown until runtime — you cannot write a fixed `with a, b, c:`
`with ExitStack() as stack: files = [stack.enter_context(open(p)) for p in paths]` — all closed in reverse order
`stack.enter_context(cm)` enters a manager and registers its __exit__; returns the __enter__ value
`stack.callback(fn, *args, **kwargs)` registers a plain function to run at exit — no manager needed
`stack.push(exit_callable)` registers something with an __exit__-compatible signature that can inspect/suppress the exception
`stack.pop_all()` transfers ownership to a new stack — the classic all-or-nothing pattern: build resources, then `stack.pop_all()` on success so cleanup is deferred to the caller
`stack.close()` unwinds everything immediately without leaving a `with` block
Unwinding is LIFO, mirroring nested `with` semantics exactly
Errors during unwinding are chained via `__context__`, so no cleanup failure is lost
`contextlib.AsyncExitStack` is the async twin: `enter_async_context`, `push_async_exit`, `push_async_callback`
Use case: optional resources — `if verbose: stack.enter_context(logging_ctx())` with no nesting explosion
Compare: `ExitStack` = runtime-variable, `with a, b` = compile-time-fixed

chapters.title: Async Context Managers
points: Protocol: `__aenter__` and `__aexit__`, both coroutines, driven by `async with`
`async with` is only legal inside an `async def` — using it in a sync function is a SyntaxError
Same signature rules: `__aexit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb)` and a truthy return suppresses
`@contextlib.asynccontextmanager` builds one from an `async def` generator with a single `yield`
Example: `async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:` and `async with session.get(url) as resp:`
`asyncio.Lock`, `asyncio.Semaphore`, and `asyncio.TaskGroup` are all async context managers
`async with` supports the comma form and `AsyncExitStack` for variable counts
Cleanup in __aexit__ can await — that is the whole point vs sync __exit__ which cannot
Cancellation: `asyncio.CancelledError` reaches __aexit__ like any exception; use `asyncio.shield` or a `finally` if teardown must complete
`contextlib.aclosing(obj)` calls `await obj.aclose()` — the async-generator-safe counterpart of `closing`
Mixing rule: an object may implement both sync and async protocols, but `with` on an async-only manager raises `TypeError: object does not support the context manager protocol`
`AbstractAsyncContextManager` is the ABC for typing and isinstance checks

chapters.title: Standard Library Managers You Should Know
points: `open(...)` — the canonical file manager; __enter__ returns the file object
`threading.Lock` / `RLock` / `Condition` / `Semaphore` — `with lock:` acquires and always releases
`decimal.localcontext()` — scoped precision/rounding changes that auto-restore
`tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()` and `NamedTemporaryFile()` — auto-deleted on exit
`unittest.mock.patch(...)` — patch applied inside the block, restored after
`pytest.raises(ValueError)` — asserts the block raises; `warns` and `deprecated_call` follow the same shape
`os.scandir()` — closes the directory iterator deterministically
`socket.socket()`, `sqlite3.connect()` (commits/rolls back — note: does NOT close the connection), `zipfile.ZipFile`, `subprocess.Popen`
`contextlib.redirect_stdout(buf)` / `redirect_stderr(buf)` — capture printed output
`contextlib.chdir(path)` (3.11+) — scoped working-directory change
`warnings.catch_warnings()` — scoped warning filters; pair with `simplefilter('error')` in tests
`multiprocessing.Pool` and `concurrent.futures.Executor` — `with` calls shutdown/join for you

chapters.title: Common Mistakes and Gotchas
points: `with open(a), open(b):` where the second open raises — safe; but `with open(a) as f: ...` then using `f` after the block — closed file, ValueError: I/O operation on closed file
Returning `True` from __exit__ by habit — silently eats every exception in the block
Bare `yield` in an @contextmanager without try/finally — teardown skipped whenever the body raises
Reusing a single @contextmanager instance twice: `cm = mgr(); with cm: ...; with cm: ...` raises RuntimeError
Doing acquisition in `__init__` instead of `__enter__` — resource leaks if the `with` is never entered
Partial setup in __enter__ that raises after acquiring resource #1 — __exit__ never runs, #1 leaks; use an internal ExitStack
`with suppress(Exception):` around a large block — hides real failures and skips the rest of the block silently
Assuming `with` swallows exceptions — it does not; it only guarantees cleanup
Long-lived `with` around a whole function when you only need the lock for two lines — hurts concurrency
`sqlite3` connection as a manager commits but does not close — wrap with `closing()` if you also need the close
Forgetting `await` semantics: `with` on an async manager, or `async with` on a sync one — both TypeError
Nesting deeply instead of using the comma form or ExitStack — right-drift with no added safety

chapters.title: Choosing an Approach: Comparison and Summary
points: try/finally — most explicit, zero abstraction, but duplicated at every call site; use for one-off cleanup
Class manager — reusable, reentrant if written for it, subclassable, best for library-facing APIs and stateful managers
@contextmanager — shortest for one-off, linear setup/teardown; single-use, harder to subclass
ExitStack — the only option when the count of resources is dynamic, or for all-or-nothing construction via pop_all()
suppress — narrow, intentional exception discarding only
Decision rule: fixed and few → `with a, b`; runtime-variable → ExitStack; simple pair of steps → @contextmanager; needs state or reuse → class
Cost: `with` adds ~2 method calls per block; irrelevant against any I/O, worth measuring only in hot inner loops
Cleanup order is always LIFO across every mechanism — nested with, comma form, and ExitStack agree
Contract to remember: __enter__ raises → no __exit__; __exit__ always runs otherwise; truthy __exit__ return = suppression
Async mirrors sync one-for-one: `__aenter__`/`__aexit__`, `@asynccontextmanager`, `AsyncExitStack`, `aclosing`
Design guidance: make managers do one thing, keep __exit__ non-throwing and idempotent, and never suppress by default
Closing takeaway: `with` is not just for files — it is Python's general mechanism for guaranteeing that a paired action completes
